reader.title: Lynching of Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount
bases: A masked party took three Black prisoners charged with murder from the Plymouth jail and shot them to death in the woods (A2, A8, A10).

A 'large party' or 'crowd' of masked men overpowered the jailer, took three prisoners held on a murder charge and shot them to death (A2, A10, A13); the killing was punishment for the alleged murder before trial (A8).
A Plymouth wire report (A1, A10), Raleigh correspondence (A2, A8) and an Edenton weekly (A13) independently agree on the jail seizure and shooting of the three named men.

summary.text: The lynching of Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount took place near Plymouth, Washington County, North Carolina, on the night of January 26, 1888, when masked men took the three Black prisoners from the county jail and shot them to death.
The men were awaiting trial for the murder of a traveling jeweler or peddler near Creswell.
A Plymouth wire report carried the story to papers from Texas to Wisconsin, and a North Carolina editor called the lynchers murderers.

According to Raleigh correspondence, an itinerant jeweler named Ed. Dawman was killed near Creswell on the afternoon of December 23, 1887, and his body was left in a shallow pit, where a passing teamster saw his knees above the ground.
Four Black men were arrested on Christmas Day, one of whom confessed or gave evidence against the other three, and all were jailed at Plymouth to await the spring term of court.
The Plymouth wire named the dead man John Dawson, a peddler, dated the murder to New Year's Day, and said Spruill confessed that Matthew Blount had done the killing.
Feeling ran high, especially around Creswell, and officials took precautions against a lynching that "was expected at any moment."
The Richmond Dispatch's correspondent added that this vigilance had been relaxed over the previous ten days.
Shortly before midnight on Thursday, a party of masked men, mostly mounted according to the Raleigh special, gathered at the jail and demanded the three prisoners.
The jailer refused but was overpowered, and the men were taken to woods on the edge of town, half a mile away by one account and a mile by others.
According to the wire, the prisoners begged for mercy and were told only that they would have a moment to pray before the lynchers fired volley after volley until they were dead.
The bodies were found the next morning still tied to the trees and riddled with bullets.
The Edenton Fisherman & Farmer reported that the clothes of one of the men were on fire when they were found, apparently set alight by the gunfire.
Matthew Blount, the brother of John, was described as a preacher "of some local notoriety" who had lost an arm.
The Raleigh special thought the lynchers were probably people from the Creswell neighborhood where the murder had happened.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any lyncher or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story first ran as a Plymouth wire dispatch, dated January 27 or 28, that said "lynch law ran riot" and the townspeople were "horrified," yet called the dying men "the wretches" and presented the confession as settling their guilt.

Northern dailies such as the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Indianapolis Journal, the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and the Michigan Telegram-Herald printed it on January 29 and 30 under headlines like "BEGGED IN VAIN FOR MERCY."
The Stark County Democrat headed it "SOUTHERN JUSTICE" and spoke of sending "the Souls of Three Murderers Into Eternity Over the Usual Route."

In the South, the Raleigh special printed by the Atlanta Constitution and reprinted by the Charlotte Messenger called it "a terrible lynching" but also stressed the brutality of the murder, said the evidence was "regarded as conclusive," and remarked that everything "was conducted quietly and with system."

The Asheville Citizen went further, calling it "The Plymouth massacre or lynching," a deed done "in cold blood" for which there could be no apologists, and declaring that the lynchers were murderers who should be punished if caught.
The same editorial held that there was "only one crime" for which lynch law was excusable.
By early February the story had shrunk to one-line news summaries, one of which, in the Superior Times, placed the lynching on "last Saturday" and said the men were hanged.
Reports disagree on the murdered man's name, which Raleigh correspondents gave as Ed. Dawman and the wire as John Dawson, and on whether the murder happened on December 23 or January 1.
They also differ on how he died, by blows with an axe in the Richmond Dispatch and by choking in the wire, and on whether four men or three were arrested.

accounts.label: Plymouth wire report
accounts.gist: A masked crowd gathered at the jail before midnight, overpowered the jailer, took the three to the woods, allowed them a moment to pray and fired volleys until they were dead; their crime was the New Year's Day murder of peddler John Dawson.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondents
accounts.gist: A mob mainly of mounted men took the three from the Plymouth jail and shot them tied to trees; they were among four men arrested on Christmas Day for the December 23 murder of jeweler Ed. Dawman, one of whom confessed or gave evidence against the others.

accounts.label: Edenton weekly
accounts.gist: Masked men took the three about midnight Thursday, January 26, lashed them to trees about a mile from Plymouth and shot them; one victim's clothes were found on fire.

framing.detail: The wire said 'Lynch law ran riot' and the people were 'horrified', but called the dying men 'the wretches' and reported their guilt as settled by confession.

The Raleigh special called it 'a terrible lynching' of men accused of 'a very brutal murder', said the evidence was 'regarded as conclusive' and that everything 'was conducted quietly and with system.'
The Asheville Citizen called it 'The Plymouth massacre or lynching', a deed 'done in cold blood', and said the lynchers were murderers, while holding that lynch law is excusable for 'only one crime'.
Northern papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'BEGGED IN VAIN FOR MERCY' and 'SOUTHERN JUSTICE', the latter calling the victims 'Three Murderers'.

conflicts.note: Raleigh correspondence and the Plymouth wire name him differently; neither is clearly better evidence.
The Raleigh reports also date the arrests to Christmas Day, which fits the December date; the Edenton weekly says the body was found 'some two or three weeks since' (A13).
